newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Fed ponders risky interest rate increase.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Fed ponders risky interest rate increase.

text.p: The Federal Reserve will consider Tuesday whether to raise interest rates for the first time in 1-1/2 years at a meeting analysts called fraught with political and economic risks for the central bank.

A slim majority of international economic experts surveyed by Reuters on Monday said they expected the U.S. central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee to decide to bump up short-term rates by a quarter percentage point.
Arguing for a rate rise: tight labor markets, rising wages and an economy that is operating in an "inflationary danger zone" because it may have overshot its potential.
Arguing against: slowing growth, quiescent inflation and looming presidential and Congressional elections on Nov. 5.

"We expect the Federal Reserve to increase the federal funds rate by 25 basis points (one-quarter percentage point)," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Pittsburgh-based Mellon Bank. "But the case for tightening isn't open and shut."

The federal funds rate is the rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans. It, along with the discount rate that the Fed charges on its loans to commercial banks, serves as a benchmark for other interest rates throughout the economy.
The central bank has not changed either rate since January 31, when it cut them both by a quarter percentage point. The funds rate is 5-1/4 percent; the discount rate, 5 percent.
A rate rise now -- even a small one -- would mark a reversal of Fed policy and would lead to higher borrowing costs for consumers and corporations.
It would not be welcome on Wall Street or at the White House. U.S. stock prices jumped to another record on Monday, and a rate rise could dampen investor enthusiasm.
And President Bill Clinton is counting on the maintenance of a trouble-free economy before the Nov. 5 election to help him win another four-year term.
In a sign of what is at stake politically, 78 members of Congress Monday urged the Fed to leave interest rates unchanged. All but two of the lawmakers are Democrats.

In a letter to Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, the group, which includes House Democratic Leader Dick Gephardt from Missouri, saw a lack of inflationary pressures and argued that a rate rise would hurt, not help, the economy.

"Our concern is that an increase in the interest rates will slow the economy and drag down wages and the standard of living for middle and working class families," Rep. Maurice Hinchey, a Democrat from New York, said.

Also weighing in on Monday against a rate increase was the National Association of Manufacturers. "In the current economic climate, low unemployment has not translated into more inflationary pressure," the group said.

The Fed itself seems split over what to do. A senior central bank official told Reuters last week that eight of the Fed's 12 regional banks had requested an increase in the discount rate, with three calling for a half point rise.
"It's a good bet there will be a pretty rigorous discussion around the table," said Chris Varvares, an economist for St. Louis-based Macroeconomic Advisers.
